problem: 3DGS gives photorealistic rendering but has no object-level semantics (instance IDs, attributes) and no physically executable collision geometry, so it cannot serve as a VLN environment. Existing continuous VLN benchmarks use scanned meshes with imperfect geometry and mostly plain A-to-B instructions.
motivation: Scanned meshes suffer from merged objects, texture seams and interpenetration, which widens the sim-to-real gap. 3DGS is view-consistent and can be labeled per object, so making it semantically and physically executable could give a better embodied-navigation training and evaluation substrate.
key_idea: Turn 3DGS into an executable navigation environment by adding manually annotated object-level semantics and invisible mesh-derived convex collision bodies (a 3DGS-Mesh hybrid) inside Isaac Sim, then build a large VLN benchmark on it.
insight: Training on the photorealistic 3DGS data transfers to real-benchmark VLN-CE: NaVILA-SAGE goes from 0.29 to 0.38 SR on R2R val-unseen without any VLN-CE data. The scenes-vs-samples ablation shows scene diversity matters more than sample count (400 scenes/120k samples gives 0.34 SR, while 800 scenes/60k gives 0.36). The continuity metrics expose problems that CR hides (ICP 0.87 vs CR 1 in a wall-hugging case).
method: Object-Level Semantic Grounding (InteriorGS): 1,000 artist-mesh scenes (752 residential, 248 public) rendered from ~3,000 views each and fit with gsplat into 3DGS. They carry double-verified manual annotations of category, instance ID and bounding box (554k instances, 755 categories).

2D semantic top-down map: annotated 3D objects are projected to the ground plane as convex-hull footprints, with door states and walls as non-traversable. The map is used for path planning and instruction generation.

Physics-Aware Execution Jointing: CoACD convex decomposition of each object's artist mesh gives collision bodies, which are authored as invisible rigid bodies in a USDA scene alongside the visible 3DGS (3DUGT USDZ in Isaac Sim 5.0). Some objects are movable or articulated.

Robot/control interfaces: Unitree G1/Go2/H1 and UAV APIs, with discrete or continuous velocity commands and RGB, depth, semantic segmentation, pose and contact events, plus collision and stuck monitoring.

Hierarchical data generation: A* trajectories on a 1.2 m occupancy map fused with the semantic map. Low-level instructions are templated. High-level ones (Add Object, Scenario Driven, Relative Relationship, Attribute-based, Area-based) are generated by an MLLM from the text map. Total 2M pairs; the test split has 1,148 samples (944 high-level, 204 low-level) over 35 scenes.
SAGE-Bench evaluation: three axes (task type VLN/Nogoal-Nav, instruction level, episode complexity) plus new metrics CSR, ICP and PS (path smoothness).
Training: NaVILA and NaVid fine-tuned on 500k SAGE pairs, giving NaVILA-SAGE and NaVid-SAGE.

setting.backbone: NaVILA-SAGE (NaVILA siglip-llama3-8b pretrain, fine-tuned) and NaVid-SAGE (navid-7b-full-224, fine-tuned)

results: NaVILA-SAGE reaches 0.46 SR / 0.55 OSR on SAGE-Bench high-level VLN, beating NaVILA (0.39 SR). On R2R-CE val-unseen, SAGE-only training lifts NaVILA-base from 0.29 to 0.38 SR (+31% relative), though the original NaVILA (0.50 SR) remains stronger. Most MLLM and VLN baselines score at most 0.15 SR on SAGE-Bench.
limitations: The evaluation is on synthetic scenes rendered from artist meshes, with no real-robot experiments, so the sim-to-real claim is not directly tested.
The SAGE-trained models still trail NaVILA trained on VLN-CE data on R2R-CE (0.38 vs 0.50 SR), so the generalization claim is relative to base models only.
Many baselines score below 0.20 SR, which makes their CR/ICP/PS non-comparable. The convergence comparison to scanned mesh is loosely controlled (10k samples, one GPU).
